EU budget: twelve hours of wrangling and “zero result” in Brussels, Macron sets an end-of-December ultimatum

The leaders of the European Union's 27 countries parted ways on Thursday, November 26, in Brussels without agreement on the EU budget for 2028-2034 or on a new loan to Ukraine, after more than twelve hours of talks [1][2]. Everything has been pushed back to the December 17-18 summit [2][6].

The extraordinary summit was supposed to bring positions closer on a package of around €1,780 billion over seven years, proposed earlier in the negotiations [8]. The leaders failed to agree, despite more than twelve hours of talks [1].

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote on social media that he had seen “zero result” and considers a deal before Christmas unlikely [2]. According to Euronews, Italy's Giorgia Meloni believes the 27 are “light years” away from an agreement [3].

The Czech Republic's Andrej Babiš called the proposal “absolutely unacceptable.” Poland's Donald Tusk rejects any budget that would push up energy prices, carry heavy social costs or weaken his country's defense [6].
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned: “We cannot and must not take on more debt” [2]. On his way into the summit, he also insisted that Ukraine receive “sufficient” support in the years ahead [6].

The decision on a €45 billion loan to Ukraine has been postponed to December: Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic still need to be persuaded to take part [7]. According to AP, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia refuse to let the money fund military aid to Kyiv [2].

Emmanuel Macron wants a deal “by the end of the year” [2]. After December 31, he says he would no longer be “politically, democratically” able to relaunch and conclude talks, with the 2027 presidential election approaching [3]. The Élysée had warned that France would not pursue negotiations beyond December without a deal [4].
European Council President António Costa is due to present a new proposal in the coming weeks [6].

Key takeaway: the European budget sets the amounts devoted to agriculture, regions, defense or Ukraine for seven years, and it must be adopted unanimously by member states: a few capitals are therefore enough to block everything, as the Czech and Hungarian refusals show [2][6].

The political calendar weighs heavily. According to Reuters, several capitals want a binding deal before May, to shield the funding from a possible victory by Marine Le Pen in the French presidential election [6]. Macron also denounces a “strategic error”: the proposed cuts, even as he calls for new “own resources,” meaning revenue that goes directly to the EU [5].

Ukraine is waiting: according to Reuters, the money under discussion (€70 billion in total) is meant to fill the hole in its finances next year [6]. Every month of delay makes the bill more uncertain for Kyiv, in the middle of a war.

France is one of the biggest contributors to the European budget, and its farmers are among those who receive the most from it. If no deal is reached in December, the negotiations could drag on until after the presidential election: you can expect the issue to find its way into the campaign.

United States: summer growth revised to 4.3%, Trump cries “record error” and demands an investigation, three weeks after his election defeat

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on Wednesday, November 25, raised US third-quarter growth to an annualized 4.3%, compared with the 3.4% announced before the midterm elections. On Thanksgiving Day, Donald Trump denounced a “record error” and called for an investigation, without providing evidence [1][5].
The BEA, the Commerce Department office responsible for calculating GDP, had published a first estimate of 3.4% for July-September. Its second estimate, released on November 25, rises to 4.3% [1].
On Thursday the 26th, on his Truth Social network, the president called the revision a “RECORD ERROR” and demanded an investigation into the figures [1][2].

He notes that the correct figure arrived three weeks too late and implies that the estimate published before the vote may have influenced it: “Why wasn't the correct number released before the election?” [3]. His camp lost these midterm elections [4].
The 0.9-point gap is unusually large, but there have been bigger ones: a 1.2-point revision for the second quarter of 2020, in the middle of the pandemic [3].
Revisions are nonetheless the norm: the BEA publishes three successive estimates for each quarter, then keeps adjusting GDP for five years as new data comes in [5].
The same day, the president's Thanksgiving posts also targeted Somali immigrants, “sharia” and his political opponents, again without evidence according to the US press [6].

Key takeaway: the president is disputing a figure that is favorable to him, on the grounds that it arrived after the election. What is being called into question is the reliability of US public statistics [1][3].

These figures serve as a compass for the whole world: the US central bank (the Fed) uses them to set its rates, investors to buy or sell bonds, companies to hire. If their honesty is in doubt, everyone makes decisions a little more blindly [5].

Growth of 4.3% is very strong for a rich country. But inflation remains at 3.8% year on year [7]. An economy running fast with rising prices gives the Fed fewer reasons to cut rates, and more reasons to raise them.
Households, for their part, remain cautious: according to Reuters, holiday spending is expected to rise 4% to 6% year on year, but mainly because prices have gone up [7].

When the Fed keeps rates high, the dollar tends to stay strong and money becomes more expensive worldwide, including for European companies and governments that borrow. And when a president casts doubt on his own statistics, markets get more nervous, which can show up in your savings invested in the stock market.

Brazil: Lula picks banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco, chairman of Bradesco, as finance minister, São Paulo stock market jumps 6%

On Thursday, November 26, the Brazilian presidency announced that Luiz Carlos Trabuco, chairman of the board of the bank Bradesco, had agreed to become finance minister in January 2027, at the start of Lula's fourth term. Reassured, markets sent the stock exchange up 6% and the real higher [1][2][3].

According to Reuters, Lula had first sounded out the banker on Thursday, as Brazilian markets had been deteriorating since his October victory over Flávio Bolsonaro [1]. Trabuco accepted during a meeting at the Alvorada Palace, the presidential residence, according to a statement from the presidency [2][3].
Bradesco is the country's second-largest private bank [8]. Trabuco will replace the current minister, Dario Durigan, in January [6].
The São Paulo stock exchange's benchmark index, the Ibovespa, ended up 6.06% at 176,799 points, its biggest one-day gain since the first round of the presidential election [3][6].

The dollar fell about 1.25% to 5.744 reais [6]. Long-term interest rates demanded on the markets fell by more than half a point, according to Bloomberg as cited by The Rio Times [6]. The day before, the rumor alone had already pushed the dollar down to 5.81 reais [4].
Right after the announcement, Lula summoned Dario Durigan and Planning Minister Bruno Moretti to launch the transition [3].
This is not the first time he has been offered the job: in 2014, Trabuco turned down President Dilma Rousseff's offer to succeed Guido Mantega [7].
For the rest of the government, Lula is due to announce a first group of ministers next week, on his return from the Mercosur summit in Montevideo, Uruguay [9].
Key takeaway: by handing the Finance Ministry to a major banker, Lula is sending a signal to investors who doubted his ability to keep public finances in check [1][4].

The challenge is well known: public debt stands at almost 83% of GDP, the wealth produced in a year, and Trabuco will have to reconcile the campaign's big spending promises with market pressure to rein in that debt [8].

Why are markets applauding? According to the website InfoMoney, Trabuco, a longtime contact of Lula's, defends Brazil's economic “tripod”: a floating exchange rate, a central bank that targets inflation and disciplined public finances [4]. An economist at the firm Lifetime, quoted by CNN Brasil, sums up the reaction with a key investor demand: “predictability” in economic policy [5].
A rising stock market and a falling dollar mean a stronger real: imports become cheaper, which helps contain inflation, and the government borrows at lower rates when long-term rates fall [5][6].

Brazil is Latin America's largest economy and a major supplier of soybeans, coffee and meat. If you have an emerging-market equity fund, Brazil often carries a lot of weight in it: a +6% day shows up in your savings.

news.2026-11-27-egypte-camion-citerne-ca: Egypt: a tanker truck bursts into flames on Cairo's ring road, 31 dead, lawmakers demand accountability and anger grows over road safety

Overnight from Wednesday to Thursday, November 26, a tanker truck overturned and then caught fire on Cairo's ring road, killing at least 31 people. On Thursday, the suspected driver was arrested and Egyptian lawmakers demanded accountability, after a series of deadly accidents that have exasperated the population [1][2][3].
The accident occurred above a tunnel, in the Al-Warraq district of Giza governorate, on the busy ring road that encircles the capital [3].
The death toll stands at at least 31 [1][3][5]. The number of injured, initially reported as 25, was later corrected to 21 [3].

According to prosecutors, a car hit the back of the truck, which overturned and caught fire; a suspect has been arrested [6]. According to one media outlet, he reportedly admitted to speeding [6]. Al Jazeera reports that it was the driver who was taken into custody [2].
Families posted appeals on Facebook to find men who had been traveling on the road and had not been heard from [2].

On Thursday, lawmakers demanded that officials be held accountable, according to Reuters [1]. The website The New Arab points to a slow response from the authorities and questions about the safety of roads and infrastructure [4].
It is the deadliest accident in a recent series that is fueling public anger, Reuters notes [1].
Key takeaway: beyond the tragedy, the accident is becoming a political issue. It calls into question the state of the roads and the oversight of vehicles carrying hazardous materials [1][4].
Official figures show a worsening problem: Egypt recorded 5,829 road deaths in 2025, 10.8% more than in 2024, according to the public statistics agency CAPMAS [1].

Yet the government has made major roads a showcase: Cairo's ring road, where the tragedy occurred, is a very busy route that circles the capital [3][5]. A fuel truck catching fire on such a road, above a tunnel, can cause many casualties within minutes, hence the question raised by lawmakers: who oversees these shipments [1][3]?
The investigation must now establish exact responsibilities, between the arrested driver and any failings in the management of the road [2][6].

Egypt welcomes millions of tourists, many of them French, and the accident took place in Giza, the city of the pyramids [7]. If you travel there, this tragedy is a reminder that the roads are far more dangerous than in France: be careful with taxis and nighttime trips.

Tobacco: Marlboro maker wants to buy Britain's Imperial Brands, owner of Gauloises, whose shares have their best day since 1999

US group Altria, which sells Marlboro in the United States, confirmed on Thursday, November 26, that it is considering a takeover, probably paid entirely in cash, of Britain's Imperial Brands. The target's shares ended up 13.3% in London, and Japan Tobacco could join the deal [1][3][4].

Altria describes its deliberations as being at a “very early stage.” It is also in talks with an unnamed third party about buying part of Imperial's businesses. No agreement exists, and there is no guarantee that an offer will be made [1].
Imperial says it has received no approach or proposal, either from Altria or from a third party. Its board would consider any offer if one arrived [2].
The same day, Bloomberg revealed that Japan Tobacco is considering buying Imperial, possibly with a partner, and then splitting its businesses region by region [2][4].

On the stock market, Imperial closed at 3,432 pence, up 13.3%, its best session since 1999 and its highest level since July 27, 2017 [3]. During the session, the stock hit 3,449 pence, valuing the group at £25.9 billion, or $33.9 billion [2].
Altria is worth about $127 billion on the stock market, nearly four times Imperial [7][2]. Its advisers are Deutsche Bank and Perella Weinberg [1].
On Friday, November 27, in Tokyo, Japan Tobacco shares gained as much as 2.6% early in the morning according to Bloomberg [4], and 3.6% during the morning according to Reuters [5].

Key takeaway: tobacco is consolidating because cigarettes are in decline. Altria depends almost entirely on the increasingly regulated US market, with Marlboro, Copenhagen and NJOY e-cigarettes [6]. Imperial, based in Bristol, sells Winston and Davidoff [14] and since 2008 has owned the former Altadis, born from the merger of France's Seita (Gauloises, Gitanes) and Spain's Tabacalera, two former state monopolies [10][13].

Why a split with Japan Tobacco? According to Reuters, a joint takeover, with one taking the US businesses and the other the rest of the world, would help avoid objections from competition authorities [2]. Japan Tobacco is also looking to bounce back: Moscow seized its Russian subsidiaries, a loss it puts at $8.7 billion [5].

The timetable is set by British stock market rules: Altria has until December 24 at 5 p.m. (London time) to make a firm offer or walk away [2]. Until then, no price is known: Thursday's rise only reflects investors' bet on a future premium [2][3].

For you, nothing changes at the tobacco shop: cigarette prices in France are set with the government, whoever owns the brand. But if you have a fund invested in large European stocks, Imperial is often part of it, and Gauloises, a brand born in a French state monopoly, would come under American or Japanese ownership.

How it works: why the target's shares jump before an offer even exists

When a group wants to buy another, it has to pay more than the market price to convince shareholders to sell: this is the “premium.” In 2022, Philip Morris offered 39.4% above the last share price for Sweden's Swedish Match [11]. As soon as a buyer comes forward, investors therefore buy the target's shares to capture part of that premium, weighted by the probability that the offer succeeds. In the United Kingdom, the takeover code requires a buyer who confirms its deliberations to set a deadline: it makes a firm offer or walks away [1][2]. As long as no price is announced, the share price remains a bet: if the buyer walks away, the hoped-for premium disappears. The buyer, for its part, often sees its own shares stagnate or fall: paying a high price in cash forces it to take on debt.
Precedents: three takeovers that reshaped the tobacco industry

Imperial Tobacco offers €50 per share in cash for Franco-Spanish Altadis, or €12.6 billion for the shares and €16.2 billion including debt [9]. It targets €300 million in savings per year and finances the deal with debt and a capital increase of up to £5.4 billion [10].
A giant takeover paid in cash weighs on the buyer's debt for years.

Philip Morris offers 106 kronor per share, about $16 billion, for Swedish Match, the king of nicotine pouches, with a 39.4% premium [11]. As soon as the talks were announced, the target's shares had jumped as much as 28% [12].
Tobacco giants buy the products that replace cigarettes, and the targets soar.
British American Tobacco completes the purchase of the 57.8% of US group Reynolds American it did not yet own, paying $29.44 in cash and 0.526 BAT shares for each Reynolds share [8].
Industry consolidation crosses the Atlantic: back then a British company bought an American one; today the reverse is being considered.

news.2026-11-27-espagne-fin-campagne-leg: Spain: last day of campaigning before Sunday's snap general election, with the right and far right in the lead

The campaign for Spain's snap general election ends this Friday, November 27, ahead of a day of reflection on Saturday and the vote on Sunday the 29th. Alberto Núñez Feijóo's People's Party remains ahead in the latest published polls, in front of Pedro Sánchez's Socialists [1][2][3].
Pedro Sánchez dissolved Parliament on October 5, after lawmakers rejected his emergency decrees on housing: the vote is taking place about eight months earlier than scheduled [4].

The latest 40dB poll for El País and Cadena SER, published on November 9, gave the PP 31.9% and 129 seats, the PSOE 29.9% and 119 seats, and Vox 18% and 61 seats [3]. An absolute majority is 176 seats out of 350 [2].
The law prohibits publishing polls in the five days before the vote [4]. Vox, Santiago Abascal's far-right party, is ending its campaign in Valencia [5].
Polling stations close on Sunday at 8 p.m.; the full official count, including the vote of Spaniards abroad, is expected on December 4 [4].

Key takeaway: Spain, the fourth-largest economy in the eurozone, could swing to the right, with a government that would depend on Vox. According to the same poll, the PP and Vox together would exceed 176 seats [2][3].

If neither bloc reaches a majority, the Basque (PNV) and Catalan (Junts) regionalist parties would once again become decisive [2]. On Thursday, CNN questioned the outgoing government about these final days of campaigning [1].

Spain is the top destination for French tourists and a major trading partner. A change of majority in Madrid would also carry weight in the European Council, on the EU budget, immigration or Mercosur.

From December 1, 2026, to June 18, 2027, imported hybrids are limited by country of origin: 191,780 vehicles for China, 170,889 for Japan; beyond that, they are blocked [1]. Manufacturers producing outside the EU, including in Morocco, will have to stay within their quota, and hybrid prices could fall less [2].
